title: Counting Bits
statement: Given an integer `n`, return an array `result` of length n + 1 where `result[i]` is the number of 1s in the binary representation of `i`, for every i from 0 to n. Follow-up: can you compute it in a single pass, in O(n) total time, without using any built-in population-count function?
realWorld: Population count is a primitive in real systems. Bitmap indexes in databases and search engines answer 'how many rows match?' by popcounting the result bitmap. Error-correcting codes and similarity search use the Hamming distance between two values, which is `bitCount(a ^ b)`. Bitmask dynamic programming often iterates states in order of popcount, because a subset's answer depends on subsets with one fewer element — which is precisely the recurrence this problem builds.

examples.explanation: 3 is 11 (two 1s), 4 is 100 (one), 5 is 101 (two). Note result[5] = result[4] + 1, because 5 = 101 is 4 = 100 with the lowest bit added.
The array still has one entry. Zero has no set bits, and a solution that starts its loop at 1 must not skip allocating index 0.

constraints: The returned array has length n + 1
Follow-up: O(n) time in a single pass, with no call to Integer.bitCount or similar

bruteForce.idea: Count each number's bits independently with Brian Kernighan's trick: `value & (value - 1)` clears the lowest set bit, so the loop runs once per 1 rather than once per bit position.
code: value &= (value - 1);   // clears the LOWEST SET bit

complexity.space: O(1) auxiliary, excluding the output array

bruteForce.whySlow: Each inner loop runs once per set bit, which is at most log₂(i) + 1 — so the total is O(n log n), roughly 1.7 million operations at n = 10⁵. That is perfectly fast enough to pass, and it is genuinely the right answer if you need one number's popcount. What it wastes is context: it computes the answer for 13 from scratch even though the answer for 12 is sitting one slot to the left in the array it is filling. It solves n independent problems instead of one problem n times.

patternIdentification: The giveaway is that the output is an array of answers for every value up to n, not a single answer — so the answers can feed each other. That is dynamic programming, and the only question left is which bit operation relates i to a smaller index. Two work. Dropping the lowest set bit gives `i & (i - 1)`, which is strictly smaller and differs by exactly one 1. Dropping the lowest *bit position* gives `i >> 1`, also strictly smaller, losing only whatever `i & 1` was. Either yields an O(1) transition and therefore an O(n) total. Recognising that a bit operation produces a strictly smaller index is what turns a bit problem into a DP problem.

optimized.idea:
Build the answers left to right, reusing what you already computed.

The cleanest recurrence: `result[i] = result[i & (i - 1)] + 1`. Since `i & (i - 1)` is `i` with its lowest set bit cleared, it has exactly one fewer 1 — and it is strictly less than `i`, so its answer is already filled in.

The shift form is equally good and often easier to explain out loud: `result[i] = result[i >> 1] + (i & 1)`. Shifting right discards the lowest bit, so `i` has however many bits `i >> 1` has, plus 1 if that discarded bit was a 1. Both are one array read and one addition per element.
code: * result[i] = number of set bits in i, for i in 0..n.
* O(n) time, O(1) auxiliary space beyond the output.
int[] result = new int[n + 1];   // result[0] = 0 already
// i & (i - 1) clears i's lowest set bit, so it has exactly one fewer 1,
// and it is strictly smaller than i — already computed.
/** The same thing via the shift recurrence. Identical complexity. */
// i >> 1 drops the lowest bit; add it back if it was a 1.
int doubled = i << 1;        // shift left  -> multiply by 2
int halved  = i >> 1;        // 0000 0110 = 6  <-- the shift recurrence's smaller index
int lowBit  = i & 1;         // 1 — the bit the shift discarded, added back
int cleared = i & (i - 1);   // 0000 1100 = 12 <-- one fewer 1: result[13] = result[12] + 1
int lowest  = i & -i;        // isolate the lowest set bit
int zero    = i ^ i;         // XOR is its own inverse

commonMistakes: Allocating `new int[n]` instead of `new int[n + 1]`. The answer covers 0 through n inclusive, so the array has n + 1 slots — and the n = 0 case must still return `[0]`, not an empty array.
Starting the DP loop at i = 0. `0 & -1` is 0, so `result[0] = result[0] + 1` sets it to 1 and every later answer inherits the error. Leave `result[0]` at its default 0 and start at 1.

Using `result[i / 2]` with a signed value elsewhere in similar code. Here `i` is non-negative so `i >> 1` and `i / 2` agree, but on negative values `>>` rounds towards negative infinity while `/` rounds towards zero — a difference that silently corrupts bit-counting loops on negatives.
Recomputing with Kernighan's loop inside the DP loop, which reintroduces the log factor you just removed. The whole point is that the transition is O(1).

Calling `Integer.bitCount` and stopping there. It is the correct production answer and worth naming — but it is also explicitly what the follow-up forbids, because the exercise is the recurrence, not the result.
